item.title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
item.abstract: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. Before getting started, you need: You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post. AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘ fix the loop, not the code ’ apply to an autonomous run. The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. To open it, clone the repository locally, then in Kiro open a folder and select the repository root (the folder containing .kiro/). Kiro loads the skills and steering automatically, with fuller steps in “Getting started.” The workspace separates a shared methodology layer from the individual projects that use it, as shown in the following diagram. At the top is a global .kiro/ layer that every project draws on. Beneath it sit the per-project folders, each with its own PHP source, Java output, and specification sub-folder. Figure 1: The workspace is split into a shared, global methodology layer and per-project code and spec folders Those same shared skill files can be run in two different ways, shown in the following diagram. The identical eight-phase, parity-first pipeline can be driven either by Kiro (interactive, one application at a time) or by AWS Transform (agentic, at portfolio scale), and both convert PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java. Figure 2: The same shared skill files drive two execution paths: Kiro (interactive, one app at a time) and AWS Transform (agentic, portfolio scale). Both run the identical eight-phase parity-first pipeline, converting PHP source into parity-verified Spring Boot Java A shared, global layer under .kiro/ holds two Skills, php-model-discovery (the scanner) and php-to-java-migration (the eight-phase playbook), plus the core-workflow.md Steering file. Each per-project folder holds its own PHP source, Java output, and spec sub-folder under .kiro/specs/, so improving the methodology once lets every project inherit the gain. The single most important rule fires before anything else: Don’t read, guess at, or hand-translate a model or entity file until the scanner has run. The scanner works in a single pass with no dependencies, as shown in the following diagram. It applies three discovery strategies to the source tokens and emits one JSON manifest, with anything ambiguous routed to a review-flag queue for a human to resolve. Figure 3: The scanner runs three discovery strategies over source tokens and emits a single JSON manifest with a review-flag queue The scanner is discover-models.php, a single-file, dependency-free PHP command-line tool that doesn’t execute the target code. It only reads source text as tokens, so it runs against apps of your choice whether its dependencies are installed. It runs three strategies on every scan: Eloquent model discovery (walking the class inheritance chain to Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Model), Doctrine attribute detection (the #[ORM\Entity] attribute), and ORM XML mapping (external *.orm.xml files). The output is a single JSON manifest. A models[] array carries every field, cast, relationship, and visibility rule, and a flags[] array appears on every entry. The scanner flags ambiguity rather than guessing. For example, a $fillable list built from a runtime expression becomes a plain-English flag, and that flag list is the human review queue. Phase 0 is preparatory: it runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. The first three phases then concentrate human expertise. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. Figure 4: Human judgment is front-loaded into a preparatory Phase 0 and Phases 1–3. Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops, refereed by a parity harness The first four phases concentrate human expertise. Phase 0 runs the scanner and assembles the inventory. Phase 1 builds the parity harness before Java is written, replaying request/response pairs against both the PHP original and the Java port. The harness must pass against working PHP and fail when you break it deliberately, because a harness that misses injected breakage is not trusted. Phase 2 seeds the rulebook and gap inventory (RULEBOOK.md, GAP_INVENTORY.md), and Phase 3 stress-tests it against representative files before committing it across the application. Phases 4–8 are mostly self-driving loops: Phase 4 scaffolds the project, Phase 5 translates the data model from the manifest, Phase 6 translates the I/O layer (routes become controllers, middleware becomes filters, validation becomes annotated data transfer objects), Phase 7 converts business logic in batches, and Phase 8 proves parity against the harness and cuts over. Two principles govern the loop. First, the PHP code is the specification: the port is done when the referee agrees, or each mismatch is logged as an approved change. Second, you fix the loop, not the code, amending the rulebook and regenerating rather than hand-patching. The laravel-eloquent-sample project is a working, bounded example: a read-only slice of an open source Laravel application, with the Book, Chapter, Page, and User models migrated to Spring Boot 3.4.1 on Java 21 with Maven and an in-memory H2 database. The mapping from PHP to Spring Boot is mechanical and traceable, as shown in the following diagram. Each manifest entry on the left maps to a Java construct on the right, producing the layered runtime architecture of the generated application slice. Figure 5: Manifest-driven mappings on the left.

item.title: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents
item.abstract: AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1 , its first text-to-speech model, now generally available. The AssemblyAI-TTS-1 text-to-speech API targets voice agents running on live phone calls. In that setting, latency and pronunciation decide whether a caller stays on the line. Pricing is $15 per 1M characters , with no annual contract and no concurrency tier to buy. For developers already using AssemblyAI speech-to-text, it closes the voice loop with one vendor. AssemblyAI-TTS-1 is a streaming text-to-speech model from AssemblyAI that turns agent replies into speech for live calls. It was trained on millions of hours of audio , including real conversational data. Most TTS models represent audio as discrete tokens. AssemblyAI says TTS-1 operates on continuous audio representations instead. The AssemblyAI claims this improves realism and cuts time to first spoken audio. The launch includes a library of 4,000+ voices and instant voice cloning. A clone needs a short recording and a confirmation of the speaker’s permission. The clone in the launch post used 24 seconds of audio. Six languages are supported at launch: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian and Portuguese. There are 3 interfaces: an HTTP API, a WebSocket API and an OpenAI-compatible route . The WebSocket session keeps one connection per conversation and accepts a cancel message for barge-in. Output is mono PCM, mu-law or A-law, at 8 kHz to 48 kHz. 24 kHz PCM is the native format; telephony stacks can request 8 kHz mu-law directly. Word timestamps are included. AssemblyAI also published LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents. AssemblyAI tested TTS-1 against 5 models on 4 English sets, using 50 matched cloned voices. All figures below are self-reported , from an eval dated October 28, 2026. Independent results are more mixed. On Cekura’s benchmark of 27 models, TTS-1 scored 81.5% reading accuracy and 4.50 naturalness. Its median streaming latency, timed from the last word sent, was 159 ms. Inworld TTS-2 Flash posted 45 ms and 93.2% accuracy there, at the same $15 price. AssemblyAI also cites a 1.7% word error rate on Coval’s leaderboard . It reports a top-10 debut in Artificial Analysis’ controlled-voice arena. Cartesia’s range divides each plan price by its credits, at 1 credit per character. Pricing is per input character, including spaces and punctuation, at $15 per 1M . Every voice, cloning, word timestamps and EU processing come at that same rate. There are no per-voice fees, concurrency fees or minimums. AssemblyAI calls it the lowest-priced frontier TTS model for voice agents. However, Inworld TTS-2 Flash also lists $15 per 1M on demand, falling to $7 on paid plans. The sharper difference is concurrency: Inworld’s on-demand tier allows 5 concurrent requests. No, you cannot use it. Google fails marketing forever, so they give us the announcement and then weeks later you might be able to enter some queries. That largely invalidates my look at the Argon model and safety cards , but it can at least form a basis for looking at Carbon as well. Many eyes remain on The Hackening , as additional things get hacked. So far most of the important hacks have been by read teamers and white hats, so there has not been major damage. We are playing on borrowed time and eventually this will stop being true. I also offer a shoutout to GMO, where hackers demanded a huge ransom and they flat out refused to pay. This is The Way, not all heroes wear capes and so forth. The scariest hack was that red teamers managed to gain access to the Anthropic Slack by exploiting third party vulnerabilities. Both OpenAI and Anthropic build mainly on Slack, because no one has the time to figure out something better. Now that Anthropic is off of Git, hopefully Slack can be next before there is a disaster. Matthew Zirwas has changed his mind and is optimistic that AI will cure diseases sooner than he thought, because it can use ‘escape velocity’ and keep chaining innovations. I don’t see how this overcomes the main bottleneck of the FDA, but any time an MD gets excited by AI medical research it is a good sign. Get personalized fiction recommendations . Patrick McKenzie : This is probably obviously AI complete already, but: you get *really* good fiction recommendations, including not-the-usual-suspects, from SOTA LLMs that have a handle on you either from the Internet or through interactions. I told Claude (Opus 5.5) I was looking for a modern fantasy book and that it should consider what I’d likely enjoy but that I had likely read many of the obvious choices. I said that in an attempt to not get it to recommend e.g. A Song of Ice and Fire. It then confidently predicted about ten books that I’d probably already read, and they are… substantially more obscure. Claude was right on eight of them. Anyhow, the first “real” recommendation is already almost exactly what I wanted for the plane flight. (Tainted Cup, incidentally.) You would think Amazon would have better recommendations considering it has a) 95% of all book purchases I’ve ever made and b) full data of what I finish, re-read frequently, or barely touch, but I think Amazon just… does not really care that much about books anymore. Assuming you’ve already read Gladstone’s Craft Sequence, Abraham’s Dagger and Coin , Dickinson’s Baru Cormorant , Novik, Kuang’s Babel , Stross’s Laundry Files, Aaronovitch, Mother of Learning , and Practical Guide to Evil , here’s what I’d suggest. OpenAI : This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory. … We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole.
